*** CAPITAL CASE ***
No. 26A634
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
OCTOBER TERM 2026
____________________________________________________________________
JESSE GUARDADO,
Petitioner,
v.
RICHARD COMERFORD, SECRETARY,
FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS, ET AL.,
Respondents.
____________________________________________________________________
REPLY IN SUPPORT OF APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
____________________________________________________________________
EXECUTION SCHEDULED FOR NOVEMBER 5, 2026, AT 6:00 P.M.
____________________________________________________________________
Respondents urge this Court to deny a stay of execution, pointing at the outset 
to the State’s interest in avoiding excessive delay in carrying out a death sentence. 
Response at 2. Far from being delayed, Guardado’s § 1983 lawsuit, which raised 
significant questions regarding Florida’s multi-faceted and pervasive 
maladministration of its own protocol, has been rushed through the court system 
since the State chose to sign his death warrant one week after he filed this action.
Under Florida law, Guardado only became warrant-eligible upon the 
completion of his clemency proceedings, which occurred in August 2026. See Abdool

2
v. Bondi, 141 So. 3d 529, 539-40 (Fla. 2014).1 Guardado then timely filed his § 1983 
action in the district court mere weeks later and with the expectation that it would 
proceed along a typical civil litigation schedule and without an impending death 
warrant on the horizon. Despite there being dozens of warrant-eligible prisoners in 
Florida, many of whom have no pending litigation, the State chose to sign Guardado’s 
death warrant.
As Judge Pryor noted in her concurring opinion below, “[Guardado’s] case has 
brought to light concerning facts about the Florida Department of Corrections’ failure 
to maintain accurate records for drugs used in its executions.” App. A1 (Eleventh 
Circuit Order Denying Motion for Stay of Execution), CA11-ECF 13-1 at 18. 
Respondents now seek to avoid accountability and moot out Guardado’s litigation 
calling into question their ability to carry out a constitutionally tolerable death 
sentence. These efforts should not be rewarded. Because Guardado’s petition presents 
significant questions worthy of this Court’s consideration, the Court should grant a 
stay.
1 Both here and in their brief in opposition, Respondents defend the Eleventh 
Circuit’s erroneous definition of warrant eligibility under Florida law because 
“[c]lemency is not part of the definition in either the [Florida] statute or the rule of 
court.” BIO at 14 n.1; Response at 2. While clemency is an executive function in 
Florida, the Florida Legislature has statutorily prescribed that an individual’s death 
sentence cannot be carried out without the undertaking of the clemency process. 
Specifically, although the legislature has empowered the Governor to initiate, with 
the signing of a death warrant, the execution of a death-sentenced individual, the 
Governor is only permitted to issue such a warrant if “the executive clemency process 
has concluded[.]” See Fla. Stat. § 922.052(b), (c).

3
Respondents call Guardado’s Eighth Amendment challenge “sheer 
speculation.” Response at 2-3. On the contrary, Guardado’s lawsuit—based on the 
fraction of Respondents’ own records that Guardado was able to obtain—presented 
concrete evidence of an objectively intolerable risk of harm due to Respondents’ 
documented, routine failure to follow their own lethal-injection protocol in critical 
respects, including through the improper and insufficient dosing of drugs and the use 
of drugs unauthorized by the protocol.
Respondents rely on Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 U.S. 119, 125-26 (2019), and Hill 
v. McDonough, 547 U.S. 573, 577 (2006), to show why a stay is not warranted. 
Response at 3. But those cases differ from Guardado’s in a critical respect: in both, 
the individuals initiated their lawsuits shortly before their previously scheduled 
executions. By contrast, Guardado filed this action shortly after becoming warranteligible and prior to a death warrant being signed. The State then opted to set 
Guardado’s execution and Respondents are now calling for this Court to curtail his 
litigation owing to exigent circumstances that are entirely of their own making and 
in order to forestall further inquiry into the concerning issues Guardado has alleged 
regarding Respondents’ inability to follow their own protocol. 
Respondents also miscast Guardado’s Eighth Amendment claim as centered 
on the use of expired etomidate. Response at 4. But Guardado’s complaint alleged 
that, over the course of an unprecedented number of executions in Florida beginning 
in 2025, corrections officials deviated from the protocol on numerous occasions and in 
multiple respects—not just regarding the documentation showing the use of expired

4
etomidate. The evidentiary hearing held in the district court raised more questions 
than answers in light of significant new information that was revealed about FDOC’s 
execution and pharmaceutical practices. As just one example, Judge Pryor noted that 
“[i]t is undisputed that the logs [FDOC] maintained showed that for three []
executions, [there were] no entries showing that it had used any etomidate at all.” 
CA11-ECF 13-1 at 17-18. Such recordkeeping errors implicate the reliability of 
Respondents’ recordkeeping as a whole and call into question their ability to carry 
out a constitutionally sound execution, particularly given the pre-existing risks 
inherent to Florida’s three-drug protocol.
Regarding Guardado’s second certiorari question as to the truncated discovery 
process afforded to him by the district court, Respondents attempt to minimize the 
significance of this issue by pointing to “state confidentiality law,” because “[t]he 
disclosure of the pharmacy logs risks disclosing the supplier of the drugs.” Response 
at 4-5. But there were options that the district court could have taken to maintain 
confidentiality while providing Guardado with an opportunity to review the 
unredacted pharmacy logs, such as permitting redactions, sealing records, or issuing 
a protective order. And, indeed, Respondents ultimately filed redacted versions of the 
pharmacy logs on the public docket in the district court.
More broadly, Respondents’ concerns are belied by their past actions. 
Guardado’s litigation is partially based on records produced by Respondents in 
response to records requests. It was only after a lawsuit initiated by a different deathrow prisoner brought the errors in Respondents’ records to light that they abruptly

5
stopped complying with any requests for additional records. In subsequent litigation 
brought by other prisoners relying on those same records, Respondents dubbed 
allegations of maladministration based on their own documentation to be speculative, 
conclusory, vague, and tenuous, refusing to acknowledge that problems were 
occurring yet simultaneously refusing to share further records to show that to be true. 
See, e.g., State v. Trotter, No. 411986-CF-1225, Doc. 1101 (Manatee Cnty. Cir. Ct. Feb. 
3, 2026); Trotter v. State, SC2026-0214 (Fla. Feb. 10, 2026); Heath v. State, SC2026-
0112 (Fla. Jan. 27, 2026); State v. Heath, No. 011989-CF-3026A (Alachua Cnty. Cir.
Ct. Jan. 20, 2026); Walls v. Sec’y, Fla. Dep’t of Corr., Case No: 4:25-cv-588, ECF 14 at 
34-36 (N.D. Fla. Dec. 5, 2025). Then, just before the hearing, Guardado learned of 
new discrepancies in Respondents’ records, including the use of Wite-Out to correct 
the expiration dates for the etomidate used in six executions. See CA11-ECF 13-1 at 
19 (What is “even more concerning [than the errors in the logs] is Florida’s response 
once it learned during litigation about the errors in its drug log [by using] Wite-Out 
liquid eraser to alter the logs. It did not make any attempt to document either in the 
log or elsewhere that a change had been made to the log, when the change was made, 
who made the change, or why the change had been made.”). Respondents’ pattern of 
behavior indicates that their true concern is not that the identity of the drug 
manufacturers or suppliers will be revealed; it is that, if more documentary evidence 
comes to light, more evidence of their own maladministration will be revealed.
As Judge Pryor observed, “this case demonstrates [that] a State’s failure to 
maintain accurate records will invariably lead to concerns and questions about

6
whether the State is adhering to its protocol as well as the efficacy and 
constitutionality of that protocol.” CA11-ECF 13-1 at 20. Here, Respondents have 
never adequately addressed those concerns and signed Guardado’s death warrant 
rather than answer those questions. The issues Guardado raised are significant and 
implicate Respondents’ ability to constitutionally carry out executions in the midst of 
an unprecedented execution spree in Florida. 
The Court should grant a stay of execution.
Respectfully submitted,
 /s/ Linda McDermott
Linda McDermott
 Counsel of Record
 /s/ Sean Gunn
Sean Gunn
